prerequisites: Good foundations of mathematical analysis are required, including the treatment of complex numbers.

learning_outcomes.text: Understand the fundamental theoretical concepts related to probability theory and deterministic and random signals.
Assimilate the approach to probability and the properties of random variables (including notable distributions and the Q-function).
Deeply understand the representation and analysis of signals and LTI systems in both the time and frequency domains.
Calculate probabilities associated with random variables in general and, in particular, with Gaussian variables.
Apply the studied mathematical models to analyze, classify, and determine the time and frequency responses of linear time-invariant systems, with potential applications to communication systems.
Determine averages, energies, powers, and spectral densities.
Utilize ideal sampling and reconstruction formulas.
Evaluate/interpret the effectiveness and performance of an elementary system in the presence of bandwidth limitations or Gaussian noise.
Select the most appropriate probabilistic calculation models and spectral analysis methodologies to describe specific phenomena.
Independently interpret numerical results deriving from theoretical exercises.
Communicate the problems, technical solutions, and engineering properties of signals using a rigorous and appropriate technical language.

Clearly, coherently, and concisely present the analysis methodologies applied within the exams (both written and oral), scientifically arguing the connections between the various domains of signal representation.
Develop the capacity to independently deepen more advanced topics within telecommunications engineering.
Consult and understand specialized reference textbooks, university lecture notes, and technical documentation of the sector.
More easily assimilate subsequent courses in the curriculum that rely on digital technologies and signal processing.

syllabus_topics: Introduction to communication systems, with particular reference to aspects involving probability and random variables (source, source coding, Gaussian channel) and signal representation (modulations).
Foundations of probability and random variables: Axiomatic approach.
CDF and PDF of a random variable.
Uniform, exponential, Poisson, Bernoulli, and Gaussian CDF and PDF.
Calculation of probabilities associated with Gaussian random variables.
Pairs of random variables, CDF, pmf, and pdf.
Joint moments, covariance and correlation, covariance and correlation matrices.
Introduction to random processes, complete and synthetic characterization.
Signals and systems in the time domain: Elementary deterministic continuous-time and discrete-time signals.
System classification (linearity, dispersiveness, causality, stationarity, stability).
Signals and systems in the frequency domain: Representation of continuous and discrete signals in the frequency domain.
Input-output relationships for energy and power spectral densities.
Signal sampling: Ideal sampling and reconstruction formula.
teaching_methods: Numerical exercises solved on the blackboard
Use of the Handy platform for lecture-by-lecture updates on topics and exercises covered in class, homework assignments, and sharing of exam papers (some with solutions)
assessment_rules: The final exam consists of a written test and an oral interview. The written test is composed of two theoretical questions and two numerical exercises, each graded out of thirty, with a passing grade of no less than 18. A necessary condition to pass the written test is achieving a passing grade on both theoretical questions and on at least one numerical exercise, with an overall sufficient average score of no less than 18. The oral interview is an in-depth discussion of the topics covered in the written test. Attending students have the option to split the exam into two partial tests, each consisting of a written test and a respective oral interview, which are only valid if both are sufficient.
